10.1 Static insurance: no insurance possible (constant τ)
10.2 Two-period recursive + First Best Euler
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{10.2 --- TWO-PERIOD RECURSIVE SETUP + First Best.}}

\emph{Setup.} Two periods, iid shocks $\theta$ (period 1), $\theta'$ (period 2). Agent discount $\beta$; planner discount/bond price $q$. Continuation utility $w_n$ promised after period-1 shock $\theta_n$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Planner's recursive problem.}}
\[ \max_{\{\tau_n^1, w_n\}} \sum_n \pi_n[-\tau_n^1 + q V(w_n)] \]
\[ \text{s.t.}\;\; \sum_n \pi_n[u(\tau_n^1 + \theta_n) + \beta w_n] \geq U_0 \;(IR),\;\; \text{IC}(n, i)\;\forall n, i. \tag{10.3} \]

\emph{Sufficient statistic.} $w_n$ encodes the entire second-period continuation; static analysis (10.1) then determines $\tau_n^2$ to deliver $w_n$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First Best (shocks observable).}}
FOCs (without IC):
\[ w_n: -qV'(w_n^{FB}) = \beta\lambda, \qquad \tau_n^1: 1 = u'(\tau_n^{1\,FB} + \theta_n)\lambda. \]
$\Rightarrow$ \emph{full insurance:} $\tau_n^{1\,FB} + \theta_n = \bar c_1$ constant, and \emph{constant continuation:} $w_n^{FB} = \bar w$.

Rearrange (using $V'$ from 10.2): \textcolor{orange}{Euler equation for risk-free savings}
\[ \boxed{\;q\, u'(\bar c_1) = \beta\, \mathbb{E}[u'(c_2(\theta'))].\;} \tag{10.5} \]
\emph{Reading.} First best matches an agent with access to a risk-free bond at price $q$. No intertemporal distortion.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why FB fails under hidden info.}} At FB, each low-$\theta$ agent's indifference curve has steeper slope (single-crossing). \emph{All} agents would prefer to claim $\theta_1$ (highest transfer, same $\bar w$). FB violates IC.

nodes.title: 10.3 Second Best: LDIC binds, τ↓, w↑
10.4 Inverse Euler ⇒ positive capital tax
10.5 Hidden savings ⇒ bond economy (incomplete markets)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{10.5 --- ENDOGENIZING MARKET INCOMPLETENESS: SB collapses to a bond economy if agents can hide savings.}}

\emph{Setting.} Agents have hidden access to a risk-free bond at price $q$ (planner can't observe trades). Agent can adjust $(c_1, c_2)$ via the bond after receiving transfers.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Consequence.}} Agent always declares the shock $\theta_n$ with the highest \emph{present value} of transfers $\tau_n^1 + q\tau_n^2$, then re-balances via the bond.

For IC to hold, the planner must offer a \emph{constant} present-value transfer:
\[ \tau_n^1 + q\tau_n^2 = \bar T \quad \forall n. \]

This means the planner can only implement the \textbf{static-equivalent} of an incomplete-markets bond economy: the agent gets a constant lump-sum and self-insures using the bond.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Result: micro-foundation of incomplete markets.}}
The constrained-efficient allocation with hidden savings = pure-bond-economy allocation (Bewley / Aiyagari / Huggett style: income risk + single risk-free asset for self-insurance).

\textcolor{orange}{Why this matters for macro.} A wide class of macro models — wealth inequality, business cycle costs, optimal monetary policy in HANK (Heterogeneous Agents New Keynesian) — assume incomplete markets exogenously. This dynamic-contracts result \emph{derives} that assumption from primitive private-information and unobservable-savings frictions.

\emph{Comparison summary.}
$\bullet$ Full information (FB): full insurance + Euler equality.
$\bullet$ Hidden $\theta$, observable savings: SB with positive capital tax (inverse Euler).
$\bullet$ Hidden $\theta$ + hidden savings: only bond-economy allocations implementable.

trash.title: Identical vs Heterogeneous Homothetic: table + Edgeworth
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Identical vs Heterogeneous homothetic --- steps visualized.}}

\emph{Common setup:} $\omega^1 = (5, 1),\, \omega^2 = (1, 4),\, \omega = (6, 5)$.

\emph{Edgeworth picture}: aggregate diagonal (gray) is the line of slope $\omega_b/\omega_a = 5/6$. In Col 2 both individual demand rays lie \emph{on} this diagonal (ratios both $=1.2$). In Col 3 they fan out wildly ($0.31$ and $4.94$); the budget line still passes through the endowment $\omega = (5,1)$, but the tangencies land off the diagonal.

{{img:0|w=1100}}

\bigskip

\begin{tabular}{p{4cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}}
 & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Col 2: IDENTICAL homothetic}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Col 3: HETEROGENEOUS homothetic}} \\
\textit{Preferences} & both $U^h = x_a^{0.4} x_b^{0.6}$ & $U^1 = x_a^{0.2} x_b^{0.8}$, $\;U^2 = x_a^{0.8} x_b^{0.2}$ \\
\textit{Each agent homothetic?} & \textcolor{green}{✓} & \textcolor{green}{✓} \\
\textit{Same $r^*(p)$ across agents?} & \textcolor{green}{✓} & \textcolor{red}{✗} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1) Agent $h$'s problem.}
$\max U^h$ s.t.\ $p_a x_a + p_b x_b = w^h$, where $w^h = p_a \omega_a^h + p_b \omega_b^h$. &
\emph{Identical Marshallian structure in both columns;} &
\emph{the difference is only in $U^h$ (see row above).} \\
\hline
\textbf{(2) FOCs} (one per good) &
$0.4\, x_a^{-0.6} x_b^{0.6} = \lambda^h p_a$
$0.6\, x_a^{0.4} x_b^{-0.4} = \lambda^h p_b$
\emph{(same form for both agents)} &
Agent 1 ($\alpha = 0.2$): $0.2 \,x_a^{-0.8} x_b^{0.8} = \lambda^1 p_a$, $\,0.8\, x_a^{0.2} x_b^{-0.2} = \lambda^1 p_b$.
Agent 2 ($\alpha = 0.8$): $0.8\, x_a^{-0.2} x_b^{0.2} = \lambda^2 p_a$, $\,0.2\, x_a^{0.8} x_b^{-0.8} = \lambda^2 p_b$. \\
\hline
\textbf{(3) Ratio of FOCs} (kill $\lambda^h$) $\to$ $r^*(p)$ &
$\dfrac{x_a^h}{x_b^h} = \dfrac{0.4}{0.6}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = \dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r^*(p).$
\textcolor{orange}{Same function for both agents.} &
Agent 1: $\dfrac{x_a^1}{x_b^1} = \dfrac{0.2}{0.8}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = \dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r_1^*(p).$
Agent 2: $\dfrac{x_a^2}{x_b^2} = \dfrac{0.8}{0.2}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = 4\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r_2^*(p).$
\textcolor{red}{Different functions: $r_1^* \neq r_2^*$.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(4) FOC ratio $+$ budget} $\to$ \emph{Marshallian demand}.
Take budget $p_a x_a^h + p_b x_b^h = w^h$ (with $w^h = p_a \omega_a^h + p_b \omega_b^h$ known), and plug in $p_b/p_a$ from the FOC ratio (Step 3) to eliminate one variable. &
$r^*(p) = \tfrac{2}{3}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$.
$p_a r^* + p_b = \tfrac{2}{3} p_b + p_b = \tfrac{5}{3} p_b.$
$x_b^h \cdot \tfrac{5}{3} p_b = w^h \;\Rightarrow\; x_b^h = \tfrac{3}{5}\dfrac{w^h}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.6\, w^h}{p_b}.$
$x_a^h = r^*(p)\, x_b^h = \tfrac{2}{3}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a} \cdot \tfrac{3}{5}\tfrac{w^h}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.4\, w^h}{p_a}.$
\textcolor{orange}{Same coefficient $0.4$ on $w^h$ for both agents.} &
\emph{Agent 1} ($r_1^* = \tfrac{1}{4}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$): $p_a r_1^* + p_b = \tfrac{1}{4} p_b + p_b = \tfrac{5}{4} p_b.$
$x_b^1 = \tfrac{4}{5}\dfrac{w^1}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.8\, w^1}{p_b}.\;\;x_a^1 = r_1^* x_b^1 = \dfrac{0.2\, w^1}{p_a}.$
\emph{Agent 2} ($r_2^* = 4\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$): $p_a r_2^* + p_b = 4 p_b + p_b = 5 p_b.$
$x_b^2 = \dfrac{1}{5}\dfrac{w^2}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.2\, w^2}{p_b}.\;\;x_a^2 = r_2^* x_b^2 = \dfrac{0.8\, w^2}{p_a}.$
\textcolor{red}{Different coefficients on $w^h$ across agents.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(5) Market clearing for $A$} \emph{(the pivot step)} &
$\sum_h x_a^h = \dfrac{0.4 (w^1 + w^2)}{p_a} = \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.4\,(p_a \omega_a + p_b \omega_b) = p_a \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.4(6 p_a + 5 p_b) = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 2 p_b = 3.6 p_a.$
\textcolor{orange}{Truly depends on aggregate $\omega$!} &
$\sum_h x_a^h = \dfrac{0.2\, w^1 + 0.8\, w^2}{p_a} = \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.2(5 p_a + p_b) + 0.8(p_a + 4 p_b) = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 1.8 p_a + 3.4 p_b = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 3.4 p_b = 4.2 p_a.$
\textcolor{red}{Individual $\omega^h$ enter \emph{separately}.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(6) Equilibrium prices} &
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 3.6/2 = 1.8.$
\emph{Normalize:} $\hat p_a = 1$, $\hat p_b = 1.8.$ &
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 4.2/3.4 \approx 1.235.$
\emph{Normalize:} $\hat p_a = 1$, $\hat p_b \approx 1.235.$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(7) Wealths at CE} &
$w^1 = 5 + 1.8 = 6.8$, $w^2 = 1 + 7.2 = 8.2$. &
$w^1 = 5 + 1.235 = 6.235$, $w^2 = 1 + 4.94 = 5.94$. \\
\hline
\textbf{(8) Individual demands and ratios} &
$x^1 = (0.4 \cdot 6.8,\, 0.6 \cdot 6.8 / 1.8) = (2.72,\, 2.267)$.
$x^2 = (3.28,\, 2.733)$.
\emph{Ratios:} $2.72/2.267 = 1.2$;\; $3.28/2.733 = 1.2$.
\textcolor{orange}{Both $= \omega_a/\omega_b = 1.2$.} &
$x^1 \approx (0.2 \cdot 6.235,\; 0.8 \cdot 6.235 / 1.235) \approx (1.247,\, 4.039)$.
$x^2 \approx (4.752,\, 0.962)$.
\emph{Ratios:} $1.247/4.039 \approx 0.31$;\; $4.752/0.962 \approx 4.94$.
\textcolor{red}{Wildly different; neither $= 1.2$.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(*) Swap test} \;($\omega^1 \leftrightarrow \omega^2$, same aggregate) &
Identical agents $\Rightarrow$ swapping is a relabel: clearing equation \emph{unchanged}.
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 1.8$ (\textcolor{green}{unchanged}).
\textcolor{orange}{Distribution irrelevant.} &
After swap: $0.2(p_a + 4 p_b) + 0.8(5 p_a + p_b) = 6 p_a \Rightarrow 4.2 p_a + 1.6 p_b = 6 p_a \Rightarrow \hat p_b/\hat p_a = 1.125$.
\textcolor{red}{Prices change from $1.235$ to $1.125$.}
Distribution \textcolor{red}{matters}. \\
\end{tabular}

trash.title: Application: Cobb-Douglas Preferences (U = sqrt(x y))
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{COBB-DOUGLAS PREFERENCES --- the $U = \sqrt{xy}$ benchmark.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Definition.}}
\[ \boxed{\;U(x, y) \;=\; \sqrt{x\, y} \;=\; x^{1/2}\, y^{1/2}.\;} \]
\emph{Symmetric Cobb-Douglas} with equal weights on both goods. General form: $U = x^{\alpha} y^{1-\alpha}$ for $\alpha \in (0,1)$. The $\sqrt{xy}$ case is the natural ``balanced taste'' benchmark: the agent treats both goods symmetrically and spends \emph{half} of wealth on each.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- Derive the Marshallian demand.}}

$\max \sqrt{xy}$ s.t.\ $p_x x + p_y y = w$. Take the log for convenience: $\max \tfrac{1}{2}\ln x + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln y$. FOCs:
\[ \dfrac{1}{2x} = \lambda p_x, \qquad \dfrac{1}{2y} = \lambda p_y. \]
Divide $\to$ \emph{FOC ratio} (the homothetic property):
\[ \dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{p_x}{p_y} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_x x = p_y y. \]
Combine with the budget $p_x x + p_y y = w$: $\;2 p_x x = w$ and $\;2 p_y y = w$. So:
\[ \boxed{\;x^*(p, w) = \dfrac{w}{2 p_x}, \qquad y^*(p, w) = \dfrac{w}{2 p_y}.\;} \]
\emph{General Cobb-Douglas} $U = x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}$: same derivation gives $x^* = \alpha w/p_x,\; y^* = (1-\alpha) w/p_y$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 2 --- Six key properties.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) Constant expenditure shares.} $p_x x^* = w/2$, $p_y y^* = w/2$. Half-half, \emph{independent of prices and wealth}. \textcolor{orange}{Hallmark of $\sqrt{xy}$.}

$\bullet$ \textbf{(2) Demand linear in wealth (homothetic).} $x^*(p, w) = \xi_x(p) \cdot w$ with $\xi_x(p) = 1/(2 p_x)$. Wealth elasticity $\epsilon_{i,w} = 1$ for both goods.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(3) Wealth-free demand ratio.} $\dfrac{x^*}{y^*} = \dfrac{p_y}{p_x}$ --- pure function of prices, no $w$. \emph{Identical ratio across agents at the same prices.}

$\bullet$ \textbf{(4) Unit elasticity of substitution.} $\sigma = 1$: a $1\%$ rise in the price ratio induces a $1\%$ adjustment in the quantity ratio. CES family at $\rho = 0$ (limit).

$\bullet$ \textbf{(5) Zero cross-price effect at fixed wealth.} $\;\partial x^*/\partial p_y = 0\;$ since $p_y$ doesn't appear in $w/(2 p_x)$. \textcolor{orange}{This is unique to Cobb-Douglas} (substitution and income effects exactly cancel --- see Slutsky derivation below).

$\bullet$ \textbf{(6) Indirect utility separable.} $v(p, w) = \dfrac{w}{2 \sqrt{p_x p_y}}$. \emph{Linear in $w$} (Gorman aggregation with $B(p) = 1/(2\sqrt{p_x p_y})$).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 3 --- Slutsky decomposition (cross-price).}}

We can show \emph{why} $\partial y^*/\partial p_x = 0$ even though the substitution and income effects individually are nonzero. Slutsky:
\[ \underbrace{\dfrac{\partial y^*}{\partial p_x}}_{=\,0\text{ (Marshall)}} \;=\; \underbrace{S_{yx}}_{\text{substitution}} \;-\; \underbrace{x^* \cdot \dfrac{\partial y^*}{\partial w}}_{\text{income effect}}. \]
$S_{yx} = \partial y^h(p, \bar U)/\partial p_x$ (Hicksian, $>0$ for substitutes). Income effect: $x^* \cdot \partial y^*/\partial w = \dfrac{w}{2 p_x} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2 p_y} = \dfrac{w}{4 p_x p_y} = S_{yx}$.
\textcolor{orange}{Substitution and income effects are exactly equal in magnitude}, so the Marshallian cross-price effect vanishes. This is a Cobb-Douglas-specific cancellation (it relies on constant shares).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 4 --- Geometric reading.}}

Indifference curves: $\sqrt{xy} = \bar U \Leftrightarrow xy = \bar U^2$ --- \emph{symmetric hyperbolas} about the $45^\circ$ line. Higher $U$ pushes the hyperbola outward.

\textbf{Optimum geometry:} the IC tangent to the budget at $\bigl(\frac{w}{2p_x}, \frac{w}{2p_y}\bigr)$. This point lies on the ray from origin with slope $y/x = p_x/p_y$ --- the price ratio. As wealth scales, the optimal bundle slides outward along the same ray (homothetic income expansion path).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 5 --- MRS and the equimarginal condition.}}

$\text{MRS}_{xy} = -\dfrac{\partial U/\partial x}{\partial U/\partial y} = -\dfrac{y}{x}$ (taking $|MRS|$). At interior optimum: $\dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{p_x}{p_y}$, equivalently $\dfrac{MU_x}{p_x} = \dfrac{MU_y}{p_y}$ (equimarginal per dollar).

\emph{Geometric reading:} the MRS depends on the \emph{ratio} of consumption, not the levels --- the canonical homothetic property.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 6 --- Multi-agent CE.}}

With $H$ identical agents (same $\sqrt{xy}$), aggregate demand:
\[ \sum_h x^{h*} = \dfrac{1}{2 p_x} \sum_h w^h = \dfrac{W}{2 p_x}, \quad \sum_h y^{h*} = \dfrac{W}{2 p_y}. \]
\textbf{Clearing} for good $x$: $W/(2 p_x) = \omega_x$ where $W = p_x \omega_x + p_y \omega_y$ (total wealth = total endowment value). Solving: $p_x \omega_x + p_y \omega_y = 2 p_x \omega_x \Rightarrow p_y \omega_y = p_x \omega_x \Rightarrow$
\[ \boxed{\;\dfrac{p_x}{p_y} \;=\; \dfrac{\omega_y}{\omega_x}.\;} \]
The equilibrium price ratio equals the \emph{inverse} of the aggregate endowment ratio --- scarce good $\Rightarrow$ high price. Distribution-invariant by homotheticity + identical preferences.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 7 --- Numerical CE example.}}

Two agents with $\sqrt{xy}$ preferences. Endowments $\omega^1 = (4, 6),\; \omega^2 = (8, 2)$. Aggregate $\omega = (12, 8)$.

$\bullet$ Price ratio from clearing: $p_x/p_y = \omega_y/\omega_x = 8/12 = 2/3$. Normalize $p_y = 1 \Rightarrow p_x = 2/3$.
$\bullet$ Wealths: $w^1 = (2/3)(4) + 1(6) = 8.67$; $w^2 = (2/3)(8) + 1(2) = 7.33$.
$\bullet$ Demands: $x^{1*} = w^1/(2 \cdot 2/3) = 8.67/1.33 \approx 6.5$, $\;y^{1*} = w^1/2 \approx 4.33$.
$\bullet$ Similarly $x^{2*} \approx 5.5$, $y^{2*} \approx 3.67$.
$\bullet$ Check: $x^{1*} + x^{2*} = 12 = \omega_x$ ✓; $y^{1*} + y^{2*} = 8 = \omega_y$ ✓.
$\bullet$ Demand ratios: $x^{1*}/y^{1*} = 6.5/4.33 = 1.5$; $x^{2*}/y^{2*} = 5.5/3.67 = 1.5$. Both = $\omega_x/\omega_y = 12/8 = 1.5$. \textcolor{orange}{Same ratio across agents = aggregate ratio.} ✓ (homothetic-result, all three from same family)

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this matters.}}
$\bullet$ \textcolor{orange}{Macro and IO benchmark.} Cobb-Douglas is the most common functional form due to constant-share simplicity. The $\sqrt{xy}$ case is the symmetric ``no preference asymmetry'' default.
$\bullet$ \textcolor{orange}{Empirical demand systems.} AIDS, translog reduce to Cobb-Douglas in limiting cases.
$\bullet$ \textcolor{orange}{Production theory.} Cobb-Douglas production functions (same math, different interpretation) underlie growth theory, total factor productivity, capital-labor substitution.
$\bullet$ \textcolor{orange}{CES family anchor.} $\sigma = 1$ benchmark; perfect substitutes ($\sigma=\infty$) and Leontief ($\sigma=0$) sit on either side.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Contrast across utility families.}}
\begin{tabular}{l|c|c|c}
& \textbf{Cobb-Douglas $\sqrt{xy}$} & \textbf{Quasilinear} & \textbf{Perfect substitutes} \\
\hline
$\sigma$ & $1$ & --- (numeraire flat) & $\infty$ \\
$\epsilon_{i,w}$ & $1$ both & $0$ non-num.; $\infty$ num. & $1$ for chosen \\
Demand structure & $w/(2 p_i)$ & $x_i^*(p)$ non-num. & corner: all on cheaper good \\
Cross-price (Marsh.) & $0$ (CD property) & $0$ (in QL too) & extreme \\
Interior in $x_i$? & ✓ always & ✓ if $w > \underline{w}$ & ✗ (price-corner) \\
Gorman aggregation & ✓ ($B = 1/(2\sqrt{p_x p_y})$) & ✓ ($B = \alpha$) & ✓ degenerate \\
Dist.-invariance of CE prices? & ✓ & ✓ stronger & ✓ \\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-references.}}
$\bullet$ \emph{Application: Homothetic Preferences} --- $\sqrt{xy}$ is the canonical homothetic example; properties (i) and (ii) both hold when all agents share it.
$\bullet$ \emph{Application: Quasilinear Preferences} --- compare cross-price-effect-zero behaviour (both kill it, for different reasons).
$\bullet$ \emph{Application: Real Endowments} --- the Endowment Slutsky equation simplifies elegantly under $\sqrt{xy}$ since $\partial y^*/\partial p_x|_w = 0$.
$\bullet$ \emph{Representative Agent Assumption} --- Cobb-Douglas is the textbook case for exact aggregation.
